prerequisites.title: Vectors and components
prerequisites.explanation: Choose axes and resolve a vector: Fx = F cos(theta), Fy = F sin(theta), with theta from +x. Components replace the vector in an equation; never add them again to the original.

prerequisites.title: SI units
prerequisites.explanation: Convert mass to kg and time to s before using force in N. One newton equals one kg m/s²; impulse uses N s.

prerequisites.title: Velocity versus acceleration
prerequisites.explanation: Velocity describes current motion; acceleration describes its rate of change. A rightward object may have leftward acceleration and slow down.

prerequisites.title: Basic algebra
prerequisites.explanation: In F = ma, divide both sides by positive m to find a. In T - mg = ma, add mg to both sides before substituting values.

concepts.title: Inertia and the first law
goals: Explain inertia and the first law
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: A released object keeps its velocity unless interactions change it. Inertia is resistance to a change in velocity; it is not a forward force.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Inertial frame; net force zero implies constant velocity.
concepts.worked_example: A puck released at 3 m/s on ideal ice stays at 3 m/s when horizontal resistance is absent.

concepts.title: Force, mass and acceleration
goals: Explain force, mass and acceleration
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: Net force controls the change of velocity. Its direction gives acceleration, which need not point along the current velocity.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Constant positive mass: sum F = ma, with SI units N, kg, m/s².
concepts.worked_example: A 2 kg trolley under 6 N net force accelerates at 3 m/s².

concepts.title: Interaction pairs
goals: Explain interaction pairs
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: An interaction has two forces of equal magnitude and opposite direction on two different bodies. Draw each body separately.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Simultaneous pair F_AB = -F_BA; masses need not match.
concepts.worked_example: A hand pushes a wall with 20 N; the wall pushes the hand with 20 N.

concepts.title: Normal force and free-body diagrams
goals: Explain normal force and free-body diagrams
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: Select one body, then list external interactions on it. The normal acts perpendicular to contact and is determined by the perpendicular equation of motion.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Horizontal support, upward acceleration a: N - mg = ma. Contact must remain.
concepts.worked_example: A 50 kg passenger accelerating upward at 2 m/s² has N = 600 N for g = 10 m/s².

concepts.title: Tension and connected bodies
goals: Explain tension and connected bodies
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: A taut rope pulls along its length. Equal tension follows from a massless rope over a frictionless massless pulley, not from the word rope alone.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Ideal taut inextensible rope and pulley; for upward moving mass: T - mg = ma.
concepts.worked_example: A 2 kg mass accelerating upward at 1 m/s² needs 22 N tension, with g = 10.

concepts.title: Concurrent-force equilibrium
goals: Explain concurrent-force equilibrium
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: For a particle in equilibrium, vector components sum to zero. Forces can be nonzero individually. Constant velocity also permits equilibrium.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Particle/concurrent forces; sum Fx = sum Fy = 0.
concepts.worked_example: Forces 3 N east and 4 N north are balanced by 5 N southwest with components -3 and -4 N.

concepts.title: Static friction
goals: Explain static friction
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: At a sticking contact, friction supplies the required tangential force up to a limit. Determine the needed friction before comparing with the maximum.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Dry contact model: |fs| ≤ mu_s N; equality only at impending slip.
concepts.worked_example: A 2 kg box pushed by 3 N stays still if mu_s = 0.4 and g = 10; friction is 3 N, not 8 N.

concepts.title: Kinetic and rolling friction
goals: Explain kinetic and rolling friction
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: Sliding friction opposes relative sliding at contact. Rolling resistance involves deformation and dissipation; ideal pure rolling need not dissipate energy or require nonzero friction.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Dry sliding approximation fk = mu_k N. There is no universal rolling-resistance coefficient law here.
concepts.worked_example: A 5 kg crate sliding right with mu_k = 0.2 has 10 N friction left when g = 10 and N = mg.

concepts.title: Momentum and conservation
goals: Explain momentum and conservation
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: Momentum is a vector attached to the chosen system. Internal interaction pairs cancel in the system sum. External impulse determines whether total momentum changes.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Fixed system: delta P = external impulse. Conservation requires zero net external impulse over the interval.
concepts.worked_example: Two skaters push apart on ideal ice; their total horizontal momentum remains its initial value.

concepts.title: Impulse and force-time graphs
goals: Explain impulse and force-time graphs
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: Impulse measures force accumulated over time and equals change in momentum. Area under a signed force-time graph determines the signed impulse.
concepts.formula_assumptions: J = integral F dt = delta p; constant-force shortcut J = F delta t.
concepts.worked_example: A constant 4 N force lasting 3 s gives 12 N s impulse.

concepts.title: Uniform circular dynamics
goals: Explain uniform circular dynamics
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: Speed can be constant while velocity changes direction. The inward resultant is supplied by actual interactions such as tension, gravity or friction.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Uniform circle: a = v²/r, r > 0. Do not add an extra centripetal interaction to the diagram.
concepts.worked_example: At 4 m/s on a 2 m radius, acceleration is 8 m/s² inward.

concepts.title: Level and banked roads
goals: Explain level and banked roads
Choose the system and justify a prediction
concepts.explanation: On a level road lateral static friction supplies the turn. On a frictionless banked road the inward component of the normal provides it.
concepts.formula_assumptions: Level: v²/r ≤ mu_s g. Ideal bank: tan(theta) = v²/(rg); no vertical acceleration.
concepts.worked_example: At r = 20 m, g = 10, tan(theta) = 0.5, the ideal bank speed is 10 m/s.

flashcards.front: Explain inertia and the first law and state one assumption.
flashcards.back: A released object keeps its velocity unless interactions change it. Inertia is resistance to a change in velocity; it is not a forward force. Inertial frame; net force zero implies constant velocity.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: A spacecraft coasts with engines off far from other bodies. Its velocity:
flashcards.back: In the ideal isolated inertial frame there is no resultant to change velocity.

flashcards.front: Interpret the diagram: identify the shown quantities, their units or directions, and explain which law connects them.
flashcards.back: Net force controls the change of velocity. Its direction gives acceleration, which need not point along the current velocity. Constant positive mass: sum F = ma, with SI units N, kg, m/s². A 2 kg trolley under 6 N net force accelerates at 3 m/s².

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: A 4 kg cart starts from rest under 8 N net force. Velocity after 3 s is:
flashcards.back: First find a = 2 m/s², then delta v = a t = 6 m/s.

flashcards.front: Challenge this claim and explain why it can fail: Action and reaction cancel on one body.
flashcards.back: An interaction has two forces of equal magnitude and opposite direction on two different bodies. Draw each body separately. Simultaneous pair F_AB = -F_BA; masses need not match.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: A swimmer pushes water backward. Water pushes the swimmer:
flashcards.back: These are simultaneous interaction forces on different bodies.

flashcards.front: Explain normal force and free-body diagrams and state one assumption.
flashcards.back: Select one body, then list external interactions on it. The normal acts perpendicular to contact and is determined by the perpendicular equation of motion. Horizontal support, upward acceleration a: N - mg = ma. Contact must remain.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: In a freely falling ideal lift, a passenger’s scale reading is:
flashcards.back: Passenger and scale accelerate down at g; N - mg = -mg.

flashcards.front: Interpret the diagram: identify the shown quantities, their units or directions, and explain which law connects them.
flashcards.back: A taut rope pulls along its length. Equal tension follows from a massless rope over a frictionless massless pulley, not from the word rope alone. Ideal taut inextensible rope and pulley; for upward moving mass: T - mg = ma. A 2 kg mass accelerating upward at 1 m/s² needs 22 N tension, with g = 10.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: A 3 kg mass hangs at rest on an ideal rope, g=10. Tension is:
flashcards.back: At rest, a = 0; upward tension balances weight.

flashcards.front: Challenge this claim and explain why it can fail: Equilibrium means no forces act.
flashcards.back: For a particle in equilibrium, vector components sum to zero. Forces can be nonzero individually. Constant velocity also permits equilibrium. Particle/concurrent forces; sum Fx = sum Fy = 0.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: A lamp at rest has weight 20 N and one vertical support string. Support force is:
flashcards.back: For the lamp, vertical force balance requires T - 20 = 0.

flashcards.front: Explain static friction and state one assumption.
flashcards.back: At a sticking contact, friction supplies the required tangential force up to a limit. Determine the needed friction before comparing with the maximum. Dry contact model: |fs| ≤ mu_s N; equality only at impending slip.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: A book stays still on an inclined rough board. Friction points:
flashcards.back: Gravity tends to slide it downhill; contact friction prevents that tendency.

flashcards.front: Interpret the diagram: identify the shown quantities, their units or directions, and explain which law connects them.
flashcards.back: Sliding friction opposes relative sliding at contact. Rolling resistance involves deformation and dissipation; ideal pure rolling need not dissipate energy or require nonzero friction. Dry sliding approximation fk = mu_k N. There is no universal rolling-resistance coefficient law here. A 5 kg crate sliding right with mu_k = 0.2 has 10 N friction left when g = 10 and N = mg.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: A 2 kg box slides left on a fixed floor with mu_k=0.3 and g=10. Friction is:
flashcards.back: Relative slip is leftward, so sliding friction is rightward with magnitude 6 N.

flashcards.front: Challenge this claim and explain why it can fail: Momentum is conserved despite external impulse.
flashcards.back: Momentum is a vector attached to the chosen system. Internal interaction pairs cancel in the system sum. External impulse determines whether total momentum changes. Fixed system: delta P = external impulse. Conservation requires zero net external impulse over the interval.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: Two carts exchange spring forces on a smooth track. For the two-cart system, the spring forces are:
flashcards.back: The interactions transfer momentum inside the boundary.

flashcards.front: Explain impulse and force-time graphs and state one assumption.
flashcards.back: Impulse measures force accumulated over time and equals change in momentum. Area under a signed force-time graph determines the signed impulse. J = integral F dt = delta p; constant-force shortcut J = F delta t.

flashcards.front: Predict and explain: A 2 kg ball changes velocity from +3 m/s to -1 m/s. Impulse is:
flashcards.back: Delta p = 2×(-1-3) = -8 kg m/s.

flashcards.back: Speed can be constant while velocity changes direction. The inward resultant is supplied by actual interactions such as tension, gravity or friction. Uniform circle: a = v²/r, r > 0. Do not add an extra centripetal interaction to the diagram. At 4 m/s on a 2 m radius, acceleration is 8 m/s² inward.

flashcards.back: The square of speed appears in v²/r.

flashcards.front: Explain level and banked roads and state one assumption.
flashcards.back: On a level road lateral static friction supplies the turn. On a frictionless banked road the inward component of the normal provides it. Level: v²/r ≤ mu_s g. Ideal bank: tan(theta) = v²/(rg); no vertical acceleration.
